title: Marsupials
objective: After this level you can explain how kangaroos and other marsupials raise their young in a pouch.
summary: Marsupials are born tiny and finish growing in a pouch; a red kangaroo is born after about 33 days at jellybean size. Most live in Australia and New Guinea; opossums in the Americas.

cards.headline: A newborn red kangaroo is about the size of a jellybean.
cards.body: Its mother is pregnant for only about 33 days. Then the tiny baby climbs, on its own, straight into her pouch. Welcome to the marsupials: mammals that finish growing up outside the womb.

cards.headline: Born early, finished in the pouch
cards.body: Marsupial young are born in an embryo-like state and keep developing outside the womb. The newborn makes its own way to the shelter, warmth and milk of the pouch. Not every marsupial has a full pouch; in some species the nipples are simply exposed. Either way, the milk is the point: part nursery, part kitchen.

cards.fact: A joey moves out at about 235 days, but keeps coming back for milk.
cards.context: A red kangaroo joey leaves the pouch for good at around 235 days old, then keeps suckling until about 12 months. Red kangaroos are the largest living marsupials, with males standing about 2 m tall. Not bad for a jellybean.

cards.headline: Not only in Australia
cards.body: Most marsupial species live in Australia, New Guinea and nearby islands. The rest live in the Americas, mainly South and Central America. The Virginia opossum is the only marsupial found north of Mexico. Its young are born after just 12 to 13 days, about 14 mm long, and climb into the pouch. Seen an opossum in North America? You've met a marsupial.
